tagline: The prophet who watched Jerusalem fall, pleading with a people who would not listen and promising a new covenant written on the heart.
overview:
Jeremiah is the book of a prophet who lived through the end of the world as his people knew it. Called as a young man in the reign of King Josiah, he spoke for about forty years while the kingdom of Judah slid from reform into denial, from denial into rebellion, and from rebellion into ruin. He warned that the Babylonian army would come from the north, that the temple would not save a people who broke the covenant, and that the only way to live was to surrender. He was beaten, jailed, thrown into a muddy cistern, and called a traitor. Then everything he said came true: in 587 or 586 BC the Babylonians burned the temple and carried the people into exile.

The book is not arranged as a tidy biography. It gathers poems of judgment, prose sermons, stories about the prophet's arrests and trials, symbolic acts (a ruined linen belt, a smashed clay jar, a wooden yoke), letters to the exiles, oracles against the nations, and a handful of raw, private prayers in which Jeremiah argues with God. At its heart, in chapters 30 to 33, stands a small book of comfort that promises restoration after judgment and, in 31:31-34, a new covenant in which God will write his law on his people's hearts and forgive their sins.

Jeremiah matters because it refuses both cheap hope and final despair. It tells the truth about sin and its consequences without flinching, and it lets a faithful man weep, doubt, and complain in God's presence. The New Testament hears in its new covenant the promise Jesus fulfilled at the Last Supper.
author:
The book names its prophet as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth, a village in the territory of Benjamin a few miles north of Jerusalem (1:1). The book itself tells how his words came to be written down. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim (about 605 BC), Jeremiah dictated his oracles to Baruch son of Neriah, a scribe, who read the scroll in the temple; when the king cut it up and burned it, Jeremiah dictated a second scroll with many words added (chapter 36). Baruch appears as Jeremiah's companion, witness, and secretary (chapters 32, 36, 43, and 45), and many scholars think he, or scribes like him, gave the book much of its shape.

Modern study has long noticed three kinds of material: poetic oracles, prose stories told about Jeremiah in the third person, and prose sermons whose style closely resembles Deuteronomy and the books of Kings. Sigmund Mowinckel's classification of these as sources A, B, and C (1914) framed much later discussion. Some scholars attribute the prose sermons to later editors in the tradition of Deuteronomy writing during the exile; others argue they preserve Jeremiah's own preaching in the formal prose style of his day. Most agree that the book grew over time from the prophet's words, gathered by those close to him, and that it reached its final form after his death.
date:
Jeremiah's ministry began in the thirteenth year of Josiah (1:2), about 627 BC, and continued past the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC into the prophet's last days in Egypt (chapters 43 and 44). The first written collection dates to about 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim (chapter 36). The Hebrew book's final chapter reports the release of the exiled King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile, about 561 BC (52:31), so the book as we have it was completed no earlier than that. Scholars who see extensive later editing place its completion in the exile or soon after, and the existence of two different editions (see below) shows that the book was still being copied and arranged in more than one form for some time.

A few readers take the thirteenth year of Josiah as the date of Jeremiah's birth rather than his call, noting that the book records few oracles clearly datable to Josiah's reign, but most take 1:2 at its word as the start of his prophetic work.
setting:
Jeremiah lived through the collapse of one empire and the rise of another. When he was called, Assyria was failing. Josiah, king of Judah from about 640 to 609 BC, used the moment to purge idolatry and centralize worship in Jerusalem, a reform that gathered force after a book of the law was found in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kings 22-23). Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. In 609 Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt, and Egypt briefly controlled Judah, replacing Josiah's son Jehoahaz with his brother Jehoiakim. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish on the Euphrates (46:2), and Judah became Babylon's vassal.

Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC) rebelled, died as the Babylonians came, and his son Jehoiachin surrendered Jerusalem in 597 BC; the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the period, records the city's capture. Jehoiachin, the royal family, and many leading citizens (among them Ezekiel) were deported. Nebuchadnezzar set up Zedekiah (597 to 586 BC), whom Jeremiah urged to submit. Zedekiah rebelled, trusting Egypt, and the Babylonians besieged Jerusalem, broke through, and burned the city and temple. Clay letters found at Lachish in the 1930s, written by a Judean officer in those last months, give a glimpse of the collapse. Afterward the Babylonians appointed Gedaliah as governor; his assassination drove a remnant to flee to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them.
purpose:
The book was preserved for a people who had lost their land, king, and temple and needed to know why. It answers that the disaster was not the failure of Judah's God but his judgment on a people who broke his covenant, worshiped other gods, trusted in the temple as a charm, oppressed the poor, and refused every warning. That explanation vindicates God and calls the survivors to honest repentance rather than blaming their fathers or their fate.

The book also gives the exiles a future. It tells them to settle in Babylon and seek its welfare (chapter 29), promises a return after seventy years, and holds out a restored people, a righteous branch from David's line, and a new covenant. And by preserving Jeremiah's own anguished prayers, it teaches readers in any age how to stay faithful when obedience brings suffering.
story:
Jeremiah stands at the hinge of the Old Testament story, where the kingdom of Judah ends and the exile begins. Behind him lie the promises to Abraham, the covenant at Sinai with its blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28), and the long history of kings told in Samuel and Kings. His ministry overlaps with that of Zephaniah and Habakkuk, and in its later years with Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. Lamentations, placed after Jeremiah in the Christian Old Testament, mourns the fallen city.

What Jeremiah announces, Kings and Chronicles narrate, and the books of Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah pick up the story of exile and return; Ezra 1:1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22 explicitly present Cyrus's decree as the fulfillment of the word spoken through Jeremiah.
christ:
Jeremiah points to Christ in three main ways. First, his new covenant promise (31:31-34) is the Old Testament passage the New Testament most directly claims as fulfilled: Jesus speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews 8 quotes the promise in full as the covenant Christ mediates. Second, Jeremiah promises a righteous branch from David's line who will reign wisely and be called The LORD Our Righteousness (23:5-6; 33:15-16), a hope Christians see met in Jesus the son of David.

Third, Jeremiah's own life foreshadows Jesus's. He wept over Jerusalem, warned that the temple had become a den of robbers (7:11, words Jesus used as he cleared the temple in Matthew 21:13), was rejected by his own people, and suffered for speaking God's word. Some in Jesus's day even wondered whether he was Jeremiah (Matthew 16:14). This link is a pattern rather than a prediction: the suffering prophet prepares us to recognize the greater prophet who suffered for others.
reading:
Jeremiah is long and not strictly chronological, so it helps to read with a map of its parts and the kings' names in mind. Watch for the shifts between poetry (usually God's own voice or the prophet's lament) and prose (sermons and stories), and notice how often the speaker blurs, so that God, the prophet, and the ruined land seem to weep with one voice. The so-called confessions of Jeremiah (11:18-12:6; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18) are private complaints unlike anything else in the prophets; read them as permitted, honest prayer rather than as models of calm faith.

Two cautions help. Jeremiah's call to surrender to Babylon was a specific word for a specific moment, not a general rule about politics. And the famous promise of plans for welfare and hope (29:11) was spoken to a community facing seventy years of exile, most of whom would die before it came true; it is a promise to God's people through suffering, not a guarantee of individual success.

Readers should also know that Jeremiah survives in two editions. The Greek translation (the Septuagint, the Jewish translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in the last centuries BC) is about one-seventh shorter than the traditional Hebrew text, lacks some passages entirely (such as 33:14-26), and places the oracles against the nations after 25:13 in a different order. Fragments from the Dead Sea Scrolls include copies that match each form. Many scholars, following Emanuel Tov and others, think the Greek reflects an earlier Hebrew edition that was later expanded; others think the Greek translator or his source abbreviated. English Bibles follow the longer Hebrew text.

structure.title: The call of the prophet
structure.summary: God appoints Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations, gives him two visions (an almond branch and a boiling pot tilting from the north), and promises to stand with him against all opposition.

structure.title: Warnings and judgment on Judah
structure.summary: Poems and sermons expose Judah's unfaithfulness, attack false trust in the temple, and announce disaster from the north. Symbolic acts, the prophet's confessions, and words to the kings run through this section, which ends with the cup of God's wrath and the prediction of seventy years under Babylon.

structure.title: Conflict with priests and prophets
structure.summary: Jeremiah is put on trial for his temple sermon, wears a yoke to urge submission to Babylon, confronts the prophet Hananiah, and writes to the exiles telling them to settle in Babylon.

structure.title: The book of comfort
structure.summary: Promises of restoration: the return of the exiles, Rachel's weeping answered, the new covenant, Jeremiah's purchase of a field as a sign of the future, and the righteous branch of David.

structure.title: The last days of Jerusalem and after
structure.summary: Stories of the siege, the burned scroll, Jeremiah's imprisonment, the fall of the city, the murder of Gedaliah, and the flight to Egypt, closing with a word of assurance to Baruch.

structure.title: Oracles against the nations
structure.summary: Judgments on Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam, and at greatest length Babylon itself, the instrument of judgment that will in turn be judged.

structure.title: The fall of Jerusalem retold
structure.summary: A historical appendix, closely parallel to 2 Kings 24-25, recounts the city's destruction and ends with the release of King Jehoiachin in Babylon, a small light at the close of the book.

themes.title: Covenant broken and made new
themes.body: Jeremiah reads Judah's history through the covenant made at Sinai. The people have broken it by worshiping other gods and by injustice, and the curses Deuteronomy warned of are falling. Yet the book looks past the broken covenant to a new one, in which God himself will change hearts, forgive sin, and bind his people to himself permanently. Judgment is not God's last word; it clears ground for something he will build and plant.

themes.title: False security
themes.body: Again and again Jeremiah attacks the things Judah trusted instead of God: the temple as a guarantee, alliances with Egypt, the reassuring words of prophets who promised peace, and religious ritual without obedience. The book is a sustained warning that the forms of faith can become a hiding place from God himself.

themes.title: The true and false prophet
themes.body: Jeremiah is surrounded by prophets who say what kings and crowds want to hear. The book presses the question of how to tell a true word from a false one, and its answer involves the content of the message (does it call people to repentance?), the prophet's life, and finally whether the word comes to pass. Jeremiah's lonely faithfulness against popular religion is one of the book's central dramas.

themes.title: Suffering and honest prayer
themes.body: No other prophet lets us hear so much of his own pain. Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him, curses the day he was born, and begs for vindication, yet he keeps speaking the word he cannot hold in. The book shows that faithfulness can include lament and protest brought directly to God, and that God answers such prayer, sometimes with comfort and sometimes with a call to stand firm.

themes.title: God over the nations
themes.body: Jeremiah is appointed a prophet to the nations, and the book insists that the God of little Judah governs empires. Babylon is his servant for a season, the nations drink the cup of his wrath, and Babylon itself will fall. History is not the story of whichever army is strongest; it is the arena of God's purposes.

keyChapters.why: The call of Jeremiah, known before birth and sent to uproot and to plant, sets the terms for his whole ministry.
The temple sermon attacks trust in the temple as a charm and calls it a den of robbers, words Jesus later used.
The last and darkest of Jeremiah's confessions, where he feels deceived by God yet cannot stop speaking his word.
Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to build houses, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait for God's promised return.
The promise of a new covenant written on the heart, the Old Testament passage the New Testament most clearly claims as fulfilled in Christ.
King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, and the word of God is written again, a vivid picture of how the book itself came to be.
The fall of Jerusalem retold, closing with the release of the exiled king as a small sign that God's promise to David is not dead.
